newsitem.title: PERU: Peru may make key concessions to rebels - sources.
newsitem.headline: Peru may make key concessions to rebels - sources.

text.p: President Alberto Fujimori may be considering freedom for a few lower-ranking Marxist rebels in jail and reduced sentences for others in talks aimed at freeing 72 hostages held by the rebels, sources close to the talks said.

Negotiations to end the standoff at the Japanese ambassador's residence, where Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas have been holed up for 115 days, were making slow progress, a mediator said late on Thursday.
"I can tell you that small advances are being made which I think will lead to a good ending," said Roman Catholic Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani, member of a three-man mediation team.

But behind the scenes, the MRTA and President Alberto Fujimori's government are engaged in delicate negotiations over the fate of some of the roughly 450 MRTA fighters in Peruvian jails, sources said.
"There is talk of liberation for some of the small fry and reduction of sentences ... some of them may have exaggerated sentences," said a political source close to the government.
"Even MRTA has said that of its 400 prisoners, maybe 200 have exaggerated sentences," said the source.

About 20 MRTA fighters swept into the Japanese ambassador's home during a cocktail party on Dec. 17 and took all 500 guests hostage. They gradually released all but 72 of them, keeping a key list including Peru's foreign minister, Fujimori's brother and top Japanese businessmen.
The MRTA is demanding freedom for all 450 of its jailed comrades -- a demand Fujimori has refused, and which sources close to the talks said was a dead issue.
But other concessions may be in the offing, including reduction of sentences for a few convicted rebels and improved prison conditions, sources said.
Cipriani met Fujimori for two hours in the Presidential Palace on Friday, their third meeting this week.

The presence of public defender Jorge Santistevan, a Fujimori appointee whose job is to investigate cases of people wrongly convicted of terrorism, in a meeting with the mediators on Thursday contributed to signs that talks are now zeroing in on the fate of MRTA prisoners.

Direct talks between the government and the rebels broke down a month ago over the latter's demands for freedom for all its comrades. Since then, mediators have carried out a shuttle diplomacy between Fujimori's office and the besieged residence in a rich Lima suburb.
One source said Fujimori was personally leading the government's negotiations, with little input from advisers.

The 458 people whose freedom the MRTA demands include the group's maximum leader Victor Polay and New Yorker Lori Berenson, convicted in 1995 to life imprisonment for alleged involvement in a guerrilla plan to take over Congress.
